opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I admire most is how incredibly focused Noam is. He picks a problem that really matters, something that's genuinely hard and that people have been stuck on for a long time, and then he just doesn't let go until it's solved. Poker was the perfect example. A lot of people would have hopped between five different trendy topics in that time, and he stayed on one fundamental question for years until he cracked it.

The other thing is that he's very honest about what actually works. He's not attached to an idea because it's elegant or because it's his. He runs the experiment, looks at the result, and if it says the approach is wrong, he changes course. That sounds obvious, but it's surprisingly rare. And when something does work, he really understands why. He doesn't just get a number on a benchmark and move on; he digs until he has a clear mental model of what's going on.

And then there's the taste piece. He has a very good sense for which ideas are going to scale and generalize beyond the specific domain. Search and planning at inference time is something he believed in long before it was fashionable, and he kept pushing on it even when the broader field was mostly focused elsewhere. Seeing that conviction pay off has been really inspiring to me. When I was starting out, just watching how he thought about problems taught me more than most papers I read.

fable-5.1.text:
What I admire most about Noam is his patience with a problem. Most people in this field, when something doesn't work, start reaching for whatever is trending, whatever the last paper did. Noam just stares at the thing. He'll pick one idea, like search at test time, and he'll push on it for years, through poker and then Diplomacy and then into language models, long past the point where it was fashionable or obvious it would pay off.

I worked with him when I was quite young, on the poker side, and the thing that struck me was how little he cared about looking clever. He cared about being right. If you brought him an argument, he'd engage with the argument, not with who you were. That's rarer than it should be.

And he has this very clear-eyed way of asking, "what would actually have to be true for this to work?" and then going and testing exactly that. No hand waving. I think a lot of research culture rewards breadth and novelty, and he's a reminder that depth and stubbornness, applied to the right question, are what move the field.

sol-6.1.text: What I admire about Noam is his willingness to take a big idea seriously and stick with it. He has a strong intuition for which problems matter, but he’s also very empirical about how to solve them. With something like getting AI to reason through search, you can have a compelling story, but ultimately you have to make it work. That combination of conviction about the direction and willingness to let experiments shape the details is something I really respect.
